title: GrapheneOS explains locked-device extraction defenses.
summary: GrapheneOS published a clarification about how it protects data on locked devices, emphasizing its locked-device auto-reboot feature first shipped in June 2021. The post highlights that rebooting returns the phone to Before First Unlock, or BFU, mode, where sensitive encryption keys are not available in memory. This matters because many data-extraction risks are higher after a phone has been unlocked once since boot, even if the screen is currently locked. Journalists, travelers, activists, lawyers, and privacy-conscious users can reduce exposure by keeping devices in, or returning devices to, the stronger BFU state. GrapheneOS says its auto-reboot timer reduces the time a locked phone remains in the weaker After First Unlock, or AFU, state; Apple and Google later added similar locked-device auto-reboot behavior in iOS 18.1 and Android 16. The protection is not a substitute for a strong passphrase, careful border-crossing planning, or reliable backups, and weak unlock methods such as simple patterns or short PINs remain a major limitation.

why_it_matters: Modern mobile operating systems use file-based encryption, but the device’s security posture changes depending on whether it has been unlocked since the last reboot. BFU means the device has booted but has not yet been unlocked, so many user data keys are unavailable; AFU means the user has unlocked it at least once, so more data may be accessible to the operating system while the device is merely screen-locked. Mobile forensic extraction tools often care deeply about this distinction because memory-resident keys and already-unlocked services can affect what can be extracted from a locked phone. GrapheneOS is a security- and privacy-focused Android-based operating system, and its auto-reboot feature is intended to move a forgotten or seized locked phone back into the stronger BFU condition.

risks: The discussion was broadly supportive of GrapheneOS’s security model, with commenters connecting the post to real-world cases involving journalists and device searches. Several commenters focused on operational gaps, especially the lack of a complete backup-and-restore workflow that would make it easier to wipe a phone before crossing a border. Others debated unlock-secret entropy and duress-password design, noting that pattern locks are weak and that a convincing decoy environment would be difficult but desirable in coercive scenarios.
